newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine govt to propose 5.8 pct '97 deficit/GDP.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine govt to propose 5.8 pct '97 deficit/GDP.

text.p: Ukraine's government will ask parliament to set the 1997 budget deficit at 5.8 percent of gross domestic product instead of an originally planned 3.8 percent, President Leonid Kuchma's economic adviser said on Wednesday.
"We will propose increasing the deficit without changing the general economic course. Inflation in 1997 should not exceed 25 percent as we decided earlier," Valery Lytvytsky told Reuters.
The increase to four percent of GDP from three percent by Western calculations was to allow for tax and pension reforms next year, he said.
The government could cover the deficit without printing money and instead raise funds through Ukraine's first Eurobond issue planned for next year, he added.
"I firmly believe that the draft budget for next year will be the basis of stability for our currency and the beginning of growth in GDP," Lytvytsky said.
The government has not released details on how it will cover the deficit, though the original draft split payment almost evenly between foreign credits and Treasury-bill revenues.
Parliament is set to review the first draft of the 1997 draft budget at the end of the month, and the new constitution states it must pass a final draft by the start of next year.
Lytvytsky had said the deficit/GDP ratio, agreed with the International Monetary Fund, could rise by one percentage point.
Economic analysts said the IMF might agree to an increase in the deficit and it would not necessarily hurt Ukraine's request for a $2.5-3.0 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF).
An IMF mission in Kiev is set to finish a round of talks this week on the new loan and on the next tranche of an $867 million stand-by loan due to expire next year.

Lytvytsky said the deficit would be achievable only if Ukraine continued to pursue its goal of economic stability, with the primary goal of achieving 25 percent annual inflation compared with 40 percent forecast for this year.

The draft budget predicts growth of 1.7 percent in GDP next year, which would be the first increase since Ukraine became independent after the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991. --Yuri Kulikov, Kiev Newsroom +380 44 229 2264
